tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

# Agent workflow
- Before answering any question or starting any task in this repository, read this entire `CLAUDE.md` file.
- Treat the instructions in this file as active project guidance for every response and change.

# rbtree-lab: project rules
## Commands
- Build & unit tests: ‘make test‘
- Sanitizers: ‘make asan‘ Valgrind: ‘make memcheck‘
- A change is DONE only when all three pass. Always run them; show output.
## Hard constraints
- NEVER modify include/rbtree.h. It is the graded contract.
- Check every allocation. malloc can return NULL; a NULL return must
leave the tree unchanged and return the documented error code.
- NEVER weaken, skip, or delete a test to make the suite pass. If a test
looks wrong, stop and explain why instead.
## Style
- C23. -Wall -Wextra -Werror must stay clean. No VLAs.
- Error handling: goto-cleanup pattern for multi-allocation functions.
- Prefer the smallest diff that passes. Do not refactor unrelated code.
- Every non-obvious loop gets a one-line invariant comment.
## Workflow
- For any multi-file or algorithmic change: propose a plan and wait for
approval before editing.
- Commit only from a green state; message format "M<n>: <what>"

Since this is a conceptual question with no code changes involved, I'll just explain it directly rather than draft an implementation plan.

## Setup

When you delete a black node, one root-to-leaf path loses a black node. Instead of re-walking the tree, CLRS's trick is to give the node that took the deleted node's place an extra unit of blackness — call it **x**, now "doubly-black" (or, if the deleted node had no child, x is a black NIL sentinel occupying that spot). The invariant you're restoring is: *every path through x should count as one extra black to compensate*. The fixup loop pushes that extra blackness up the tree (or resolves it locally) until it either reaches the root (just drop it) or gets absorbed by a rotation/recolor.

Let **p** = x's parent, **w** = x's sibling. Below assumes x is p's **left** child (right-child case is the mirror image, swap left/right).

## Case 1 — w is red

```
        p(B)                      w(B)
       /    \                    /    \
     x(2B)  w(R)      -->     p(R)    d(B)
            /  \              /  \
          c(B) d(B)         x(2B) c(B)
```
Recolor w black, p red, left-rotate at p. w's old child c becomes the new sibling of x, and c is black (since w was red, its children must be black) — so you've landed in case 2, 3, or 4. No deficiency is fixed yet.

**Why black-height is preserved:** before the rotation, every path through w had to pass through w(red, contributes 0) then eventually through c or d. After swapping p→red and w→black and rotating, every path that used to go "through p, then w" now goes "through w, then p" — but since the colors swapped along with the positions, each path's black-count is unchanged. This is the general rule for any color-swap rotation: a rotation only preserves black-height if the two nodes trading ancestor/descendant roles also trade the colors that make up the difference. Here p gives up its black to w, and w gives its red to p, so the total black count on every path through this subtree is identical before and after.

## Case 2 — w is black, both of w's children are black

```
        p(?)                      p(?)
       /    \                    /    \
     x(2B)  w(B)      -->      x(B)   w(R)
            /  \                      /  \
          c(B) d(B)                 c(B) d(B)
```
Recolor w red — no rotation. Now every path through w is one black shorter, matching x's side (which is short by one). The deficiency hasn't been *fixed*, it's been **relocated to p**: if p was red, color it black and stop (that black absorbs the deficiency). If p was already black, p is now the new x and the loop continues upward.

**Why this preserves black-height (of the tree, not the subtree):** paths through w lose exactly one black (w: black→red), which exactly matches the extra black that x's path was already "owed." So x's subtree and w's subtree now agree, and the imbalance is pushed up rather than eliminated — nothing here changes the black-height as measured from above p, since p itself hasn't changed color yet (in the continue case) or absorbs it for free (in the terminate case).

## Case 3 — w black, w's near child (left) red, far child (right) black

```
        p(?)                        p(?)
       /    \                      /    \
     x(2B)  w(B)        -->      x(2B)  c(B)
            /  \                          \
          c(R) d(B)                       w(R)
                                             \
                                            d(B)
```
Recolor c black, w red, right-rotate at w. This is entirely local to w's subtree — x's deficiency is untouched, but now the sibling of x is c, and c's **far** child (w) is red. That's exactly the setup for case 4.

**Why black-height is preserved:** same color-swap-plus-rotation logic as case 1, applied one level down. c and w trade positions (c rises to where w was, w drops to being c's child); c also picks up w's old black color and w becomes red. Every path from p's perspective that went "p→w→c→..." or "p→w→d" still sees the same black count — you've just relabeled which node is on top so that case 4's rotation will work.

## Case 4 — w black, w's far child (right) red (the terminating case)

```
        p(c1)                       w(c1)
       /    \                      /    \
     x(2B)  w(B)        -->      p(B)   d(B)
            /  \                 /  \
          c(?) d(R)            x(B) c(?)
```
Recolor: w takes p's original color, p becomes black, d (w's red far child) becomes black. Left-rotate at p. x is no longer doubly-black — loop terminates (then unconditionally color the root black, in case it got recolored red somewhere).

**Why black-height is preserved *and* the deficiency is resolved:**
- w inherits p's exact color, so every path that used to go through p and continue past w (to d, or previously through c) sees no net color change at that level — w is now doing the job p used to do, in the same color.
- p becomes black. p used to contribute its old color once to the x-path and once to the c-path. Now, as black, it contributes one guaranteed black to x's path specifically — which is precisely the unit x's path was missing. That's what discharges the "2-black" back down to a normal single black.
- d turns from red to black to compensate for having moved up one level in the paths that go through it (it's now a child of w instead of a grandchild), keeping those paths' black-counts unchanged.

Net effect: x's path gained exactly the one black it was missing (from p), while every other path's black-count is unchanged (the color swaps between w/p and d exactly cancel out the structural shift from rotation). That's why this case both fixes the violation and terminates the loop.

---

**The general principle underlying all four rotations:** a rotation by itself changes which nodes are "above" which, and thus can change black-height along some paths — unless it's paired with a recoloring that swaps colors between the node moving up and the node moving down (or a designated child) by exactly the amount the rotation shifted them. Cases 1 and 3 use this to *rearrange* the local structure without changing anything's effective black-height (setup steps). Case 4 uses it to *actually inject* the missing black into x's path while keeping every other path invariant (the fix). Case 2 needs no rotation at all — it just relocates the deficiency upward by matching w's black-height to x's via a single recolor.

Currently there's nothing to point to: [src/rbtree.c](src/rbtree.c) only contains the placeholder comment ("I can edit") and [tests/test_rbtree.c](tests/test_rbtree.c) is empty — `rb_insert` hasn't been implemented yet. So no leak exists in the codebase *today*.

But based on the contract in [include/rbtree.h:9-14](include/rbtree.h#L9-L14):

```c
/* Copies key (tree owns the copy).
* Takes ownership of value ONLY on success.
* Overwriting an existing key frees the old value via value_free.
* Returns 0 on success, -1 on allocation failure (tree unchanged, value NOT
* consumed; caller still owns it). */
int rb_insert(rbtree_t *t, const char *key, void *value);
```

there are two spots a future implementation is likely to leak the key copy, since the function necessarily does `key_copy = strdup(key)` (or equivalent) as one of *several* allocations (key copy + new node struct, at minimum):

1. **Node allocation fails after the key copy succeeds.** If the goto-cleanup order is `dup key → malloc node → fail`, the cleanup path must free the key copy before returning -1. Forgetting that free (e.g. jumping to a `cleanup:` label that only frees the node) leaks the strdup'd string.

2. **Fixup/rotation step fails partway** (only relevant if any fixup helper itself allocates — most CLRS-style rotate implementations don't, so this is less likely, but if the design has, say, a separate allocation for tree metadata during rebalancing, the same rule applies: any exit path taken *after* the key is duplicated but *before* the new node is actually linked into the tree must free that duplicate).

3. **Overwrite-existing-key path**: if `key` already exists and the code frees the *old* value via `value_free` but then a later allocation fails (e.g. while duplicating the *new* value or key for some reason), the key copy for the overwrite case needs the same scrutiny — though per the contract, overwriting an existing key shouldn't need a new key copy at all (the existing key copy is reused), so a leak here would actually look like allocating a redundant key copy that's never freed.

The general rule to enforce once this is implemented (per CLAUDE.md's goto-cleanup + "NULL must leave tree unchanged" constraints): the cleanup label must free every allocation made *so far in this call*, in reverse order, and the key copy — being typically the *first* allocation — is the one most likely to be forgotten if the cleanup label is written to only address the *last* allocation that failed.

Want me to draft `rb_insert` now, including the goto-cleanup path that avoids this leak? That would need a plan (multi-part algorithmic function) per CLAUDE.md's workflow rule.

# Context

`rb_delete` needs to be designed before it's implemented, per CLAUDE.md's workflow rule
("For any multi-file or algorithmic change: propose a plan and wait for approval before
editing"). `src/rbtree.c` is currently empty (only a placeholder comment) and
`tests/test_rbtree.c` is empty. `include/rbtree.h` (off-limits, graded contract) documents
`rb_delete` as: "Removes key; frees the key copy and the value. Returns 0, or -1 if absent."

This plan assumes `rb_create`/`rb_insert`/`rb_validate` and the internal node representation
will exist by the time `rb_delete` is implemented (built separately, not in this plan) — the
internal design proposed here (sentinel-nil, node fields) must be the same one `rb_insert`
uses, since both share it.

# 1. Internal representation (shared prerequisite, not exposed via rbtree.h)

```c
typedef enum { RB_RED, RB_BLACK } rb_color_t;

typedef struct rb_node {
    char *key;
    void *value;
    rb_color_t color;
    struct rb_node *parent, *left, *right;
} rb_node_t;

struct rbtree {
    rb_node_t *root;
    rb_node_t *nil;          /* sentinel: always black, parent/left/right unused */
    rb_value_free_fn value_free;
    size_t size;
};
```

Sentinel `nil` (CLRS-style) means every "child" pointer is always a valid node whose `->color`
is readable — avoids scattering NULL-guards through the fixup logic. `t->nil->color` must stay
`RB_BLACK` for the tree's lifetime.

# 2. Transplant + successor strategy

`rb_transplant(t, u, v)`: standard — replaces the subtree rooted at `u` with the subtree rooted
at `v` by rewiring `u->parent`'s child pointer to `v` and setting `v->parent = u->parent` (`v`
may be `t->nil`).

`rb_delete(t, key)`:
1. Find `z` via the same search walk `rb_find` uses. If not found, return -1 (no mutation, no
   frees — delete never allocates, so there is no "leave tree unchanged on OOM" concern here at
   all, only "leave tree unchanged when key is absent").
2. Determine the node to physically unlink, `y`:
   - If `z` has ≤1 child: `y = z`.
   - If `z` has 2 children: `y = tree_minimum(z->right)` (in-order successor). **Free `z`'s
     original key/value now** (this is the moment the caller's requested key is actually
     removed), then transfer (not duplicate) `y->key`/`y->value` into `z->key`/`z->value`. `y`
     is now unlinked as a structural shell — its key/value fields are set to NULL immediately
     after the transfer so a future refactor can't double-free them.
3. `x` = `y`'s only child (`y` has ≤1 child by construction — either it's `z` with ≤1 child, or
   it's a successor, which never has a left child). `y_original_color = y->color`.
4. `rb_transplant(t, y, x)` — always sets `x->parent` correctly, even when `x == t->nil`
   (needed so the fixup loop can walk up from the right place).
5. If `z != y`: `y` inherits `z`'s structural role — set `y->left = z->left`, `y->right =
   z->right`, `y->color = z->color`, fix both children's `->parent`, and fix `z`'s old parent's
   child pointer to point at `y` (or update `t->root` if `z` was root). *(Only needed if using
   relink; skipped entirely under the copy-into-z strategy below since `z` never moves.)*
6. If `z == y` (0/1-child case): free `z->key`, call `t->value_free(z->value)` if
   `value_free != NULL`, then free the `z` node struct itself.
   If `z != y` (2-child case): `z`'s key/value were already freed and overwritten in step 2;
   free `y`'s now-empty node struct only (no key/value to free — already transferred/NULLed).
7. If `y_original_color == RB_BLACK`: `rb_delete_fixup(t, x)`.
8. `t->size--`; return 0.

**Chosen strategy (per your answer): copy-into-z.** `z` never moves — its key/value fields get
overwritten with the successor's, and the *successor node* (which structurally has ≤1 child) is
the one spliced out via `rb_transplant`. This keeps all pointer surgery confined to the
single-child-unlink case (step 4/5 collapses to just the transplant, no step-5 relink needed) and
avoids the classic "z->key lives in freed memory" bug from the textbook relink version. Since
`rb_node_t` never escapes the opaque public API, no caller can hold a stale pointer to the old
`z` identity, so this deviation from literal CLRS pseudocode is safe.

# 3. Deletion-fixup cases (x is `parent`'s **left** child; mirror for right — see risk below)

Loop invariant on entry to each iteration: `x` is "doubly-black" (or singly-red, which the loop
condition `x != root && x->color == BLACK` catches and just exits, then `x->color = RB_BLACK`
after the loop absorbs it for free) — every root-to-leaf path *not* through `x` has correct
black-height; every path *through* `x` is short by exactly one black node. `w = x->parent's
other child` is never `t->nil`, since black-height parity forces `w`'s subtree to have height
≥1 whenever `x` is doubly-black.

- **Case 1 — `w` is red.** Recolor `w` black, `x->parent` red, left-rotate at `x->parent`.
  *Invariant restored:* none of the deficiency is fixed yet — this is a pure setup step that
  makes `w` black, satisfying cases 2–4's precondition. Black-height is preserved because the
  rotation and the `w`/parent color swap exactly cancel: every path's black-count through this
  local subtree is unchanged, only relabeled.
- **Case 2 — `w` black, both of `w`'s children black.** Recolor `w` red (no rotation).
  *Invariant restored:* the deficiency moves from `x` up to `x->parent` — `w`'s subtree now has
  one less black on every path, matching `x`'s existing shortfall, so `x->parent`'s two subtrees
  agree again, with the shortfall now sitting at `x->parent`. Loop continues with `x =
  x->parent` (or exits immediately/absorbs-for-free if the new `x` is red).
- **Case 3 — `w` black, `w->left` red, `w->right` black.** Recolor `w->left` black, `w` red,
  right-rotate at `w`. *Invariant restored:* purely local to `w`'s subtree — `x`'s deficiency is
  untouched, but `x`'s sibling is now the old `w->left`, whose *far* child (the old `w`, now red)
  is red — the precondition for case 4. Black-height preserved by the same rotation+color-swap
  cancellation as case 1.
- **Case 4 — `w` black, `w->right` red (terminating case).** `w` takes `x->parent`'s color,
  `x->parent` becomes black, `w->right` becomes black, left-rotate at `x->parent`. Set `x =
  t->root` to end the loop. *Invariant restored:* fully eliminates the deficiency — `x->parent`
  becoming black supplies the exact black `x`'s path was missing, while `w` inheriting
  `x->parent`'s old color and `w->right` turning black exactly offset the structural shift from
  the rotation on every other path.

Mirror cases (x is `parent`'s **right** child): swap `left`/`right` and `w = x->parent->left`
throughout. This is the single highest-risk place to introduce a copy-paste bug (see Risks).

# 4. Where the key copy and value are freed — every path

| Path | Key freed | Value freed | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Key not found | never | never | Return -1 immediately after the search walk; no mutation. |
| `z` has 0 or 1 child (`y == z`) | `free(z->key)` in step 6 | `t->value_free(z->value)` (if non-NULL) in step 6 | Exactly once each, right before freeing the `z` struct. |
| `z` has 2 children (`y != z`, "overwrite" path) | `free(z->key)` **in step 2**, immediately before `z->key = y->key` | `t->value_free(z->value)` **in step 2**, immediately before `z->value = y->value` | `z`'s *original* key/value are what the caller asked to delete — must be freed before being overwritten by the successor's, or they leak. `y->key`/`y->value` are transferred (pointer move), never duplicated and never freed directly — set `y->key = y->value = NULL` right after the transfer as a defensive guard. |

Ordering is the highest-risk detail in the whole function: free-before-overwrite in step 2, and
never call `value_free` on `y`'s value in the 2-child path (it now belongs to `z`). Since
`rb_delete` performs zero allocations, CLAUDE.md's goto-cleanup pattern (for multi-allocation
functions) doesn't apply here — the only early-exit is the "not found" `-1` return before any
mutation happens.

# 5. Table-driven tests (priority order)

Requires a new test-only header, **`src/rbtree_internal.h`** (not part of the graded
`include/rbtree.h` contract — CLAUDE.md only forbids modifying that file), exposing `rb_node_t`
/ `struct rbtree` so `tests/test_rbtree.c` can build exact tree shapes directly and call
`rb_delete` + `rb_validate` on them, rather than depending on `rb_insert`'s fixup behavior to
indirectly produce each shape.

Write in this order:
1. Delete from empty tree → -1, tree unchanged.
2. Delete non-existent key from non-empty tree → -1, size unchanged, `rb_validate() == 0`.
3. Delete the only node (root) → tree empty, `root == nil`, `size == 0`.
4. Value-ownership spy test: a `value_free` that records call count + freed pointers; assert
   it's called exactly once per deleted key, never for surviving keys, never twice on one
   pointer. This is the direct regression test for section 4's free-before-overwrite ordering.
5. Delete a red leaf (no fixup entered).
6. Delete a black leaf, sibling red → Case 1 → chains into 2/3/4 (white-box constructed).
7. Delete a black node, sibling black + both sibling's children black, in a tree ≥3 levels
   tall → Case 2, verify the deficiency actually propagates upward across levels (not just
   terminates after one step).
8. Delete a black node, sibling black, near-red/far-black child → Case 3 → 4 transition.
9. Delete a black node, sibling black, far-red child directly → Case 4 immediately.
10. Mirror versions of 6–9 with `x` as a **right** child — catches left/right copy-paste bugs.
11. Two-children delete where successor is `z->right` directly (`y->parent == z` shortcut path).
12. Two-children delete where successor is deeper (`transplant(y, y->right)` general path).
13. Delete the root when it has two children — confirms `t->root` reassignment and final
    "root must be black" recoloring.
14. Repeated deletes down to empty, calling `rb_validate()` + checking `rb_size()` after
    *every single* delete — catches bugs that only manifest operations later.
15. `make asan` / `make memcheck` pass over a insert-N/delete-in-random-order run — leak/UB
    backstop across all of 1–14 combined.

# Risks

- **Depends on `rb_insert` / `rb_create` / `rb_validate` / the internal struct existing and
  matching this design.** None of them exist yet. White-box tests (via
  `src/rbtree_internal.h`) can validate delete's structural correctness in isolation, but true
  end-to-end coverage (insert-then-delete via the public API only) needs `rb_insert` implemented
  with this same sentinel-nil representation.
- **`tests/fuzz.c`** is referenced by the Makefile (`make test` builds `$(FUZZBIN)` from it) but
  doesn't exist yet — unrelated to this plan's scope, but `make test` will fail to build until
  it's created by whoever implements it.
- **Left/right mirror duplication** in the fixup cases is the single most likely place to
  introduce a subtle bug (copy-paste with an unswapped `left`/`right`) — test #10 exists
  specifically to catch this and should not be skipped or treated as redundant with #6–9.
- **Copy-into-z strategy** is a deliberate deviation from literal CLRS pseudocode (which
  relinks the successor node itself rather than copying key/value). Flagging in case the
  assignment's rubric expects the textbook structural version specifically.
- **`rb_validate`'s exact invariant checks aren't implemented yet either** — this plan assumes
  it checks: root is black, no red node has a red child, equal black-height on every root-to-nil
  path, and valid BST key ordering. If that's not what gets built, tests 6–14 (which lean on it
  as the oracle) need re-checking against whatever it actually verifies.

    char *key;
    void *value;
    rb_color_t color;
    struct rb_node *parent, *left, *right;
} rb_node_t;

struct rbtree {
    rb_node_t *root;
    rb_node_t *nil;          /* sentinel: always black, parent/left/right unused */

    size_t size;

# Context

`rb_delete` needs to be designed before it's implemented, per CLAUDE.md's workflow rule
("For any multi-file or algorithmic change: propose a plan and wait for approval before
editing"). `src/rbtree.c` is currently empty (only a placeholder comment) and
`tests/test_rbtree.c` is empty. `include/rbtree.h` (off-limits, graded contract) documents
`rb_delete` as: "Removes key; frees the key copy and the value. Returns 0, or -1 if absent."

This plan assumes `rb_create`/`rb_insert`/`rb_validate` and the internal node representation
will exist by the time `rb_delete` is implemented (built separately, not in this plan) — the
internal design proposed here (sentinel-nil, node fields) must be the same one `rb_insert`
uses, since both share it.

# 1. Internal representation (shared prerequisite, not exposed via rbtree.h)

```c
typedef enum { RB_RED, RB_BLACK } rb_color_t;

typedef struct rb_node {
    char *key;
    void *value;
    rb_color_t color;
    struct rb_node *parent, *left, *right;
} rb_node_t;

struct rbtree {
    rb_node_t *root;
    rb_node_t *nil;          /* sentinel: always black, parent/left/right unused */
    rb_value_free_fn value_free;
    size_t size;
};
```

Sentinel `nil` (CLRS-style) means every "child" pointer is always a valid node whose `->color`
is readable — avoids scattering NULL-guards through the fixup logic. `t->nil->color` must stay
`RB_BLACK` for the tree's lifetime.

# 2. Transplant + successor strategy

`rb_transplant(t, u, v)`: standard — replaces the subtree rooted at `u` with the subtree rooted
at `v` by rewiring `u->parent`'s child pointer to `v` and setting `v->parent = u->parent` (`v`
may be `t->nil`).

`rb_delete(t, key)`:
1. Find `z` via the same search walk `rb_find` uses. If not found, return -1 (no mutation, no
   frees — delete never allocates, so there is no "leave tree unchanged on OOM" concern here at
   all, only "leave tree unchanged when key is absent").
2. Determine the node to physically unlink, `y`:
   - If `z` has ≤1 child: `y = z`.
   - If `z` has 2 children: `y = tree_minimum(z->right)` (in-order successor). **Free `z`'s
     original key/value now** (this is the moment the caller's requested key is actually
     removed), then transfer (not duplicate) `y->key`/`y->value` into `z->key`/`z->value`. `y`
     is now unlinked as a structural shell — its key/value fields are set to NULL immediately
     after the transfer so a future refactor can't double-free them.
3. `x` = `y`'s only child (`y` has ≤1 child by construction — either it's `z` with ≤1 child, or
   it's a successor, which never has a left child). `y_original_color = y->color`.
4. `rb_transplant(t, y, x)` — **one unconditional call, no `y->parent == z` special case.**
   This is a deliberate difference from literal CLRS: in the textbook relink strategy, `y`
   physically moves into `z`'s position, so when `y == z->right` a naive transplant would try to
   set `y->right = z->right` — but `z->right` *is* `y`, creating a self-loop, hence CLRS's
   explicit `if (y->parent == z) x->parent = y;` carve-out. Under copy-into-z, `z` never moves —
   `y` is only ever discarded after its key/value are stripped out in step 2 — so `transplant(y,
   x)` alone is correct in both cases:
   - `y == z->right` directly: `transplant` sees `y == y->parent->right`, sets `z->right = x`
     and `x->parent = z`; `z->left` is untouched. `x`'s sibling (for the fixup loop) is
     correctly `z->left`.
   - `y` is deeper down `z->right`'s left-spine (`y->parent != z`): `transplant` sets
     `y->parent->left = x` and `x->parent = y->parent`; `z->right`/`z->left` are both untouched.
   Either way, `x->parent` ends up correct so `rb_delete_fixup` can find `w` from the right spot.
5. If `z != y`: `y` inherits `z`'s structural role — set `y->left = z->left`, `y->right =
   z->right`, `y->color = z->color`, fix both children's `->parent`, and fix `z`'s old parent's
   child pointer to point at `y` (or update `t->root` if `z` was root). *(Only needed if using
   relink; skipped entirely under the copy-into-z strategy below since `z` never moves.)*
6. If `z == y` (0/1-child case): free `z->key`, call `t->value_free(z->value)` if
   `value_free != NULL`, then free the `z` node struct itself.
   If `z != y` (2-child case): `z`'s key/value were already freed and overwritten in step 2;
   free `y`'s now-empty node struct only (no key/value to free — already transferred/NULLed).
7. If `y_original_color == RB_BLACK`: `rb_delete_fixup(t, x)`.
8. `t->size--`; return 0.

**Chosen strategy (per your answer): copy-into-z.** `z` never moves — its key/value fields get
overwritten with the successor's, and the *successor node* (which structurally has ≤1 child) is
the one spliced out via `rb_transplant`. This keeps all pointer surgery confined to the
single-child-unlink case (step 4/5 collapses to just the transplant, no step-5 relink needed) and
avoids the classic "z->key lives in freed memory" bug from the textbook relink version. Since
`rb_node_t` never escapes the opaque public API, no caller can hold a stale pointer to the old
`z` identity, so this deviation from literal CLRS pseudocode is safe.

# 3. Deletion-fixup cases (x is `parent`'s **left** child; mirror for right — see risk below)

Loop invariant on entry to each iteration: `x` is "doubly-black" (or singly-red, which the loop
condition `x != root && x->color == BLACK` catches and just exits, then `x->color = RB_BLACK`
after the loop absorbs it for free) — every root-to-leaf path *not* through `x` has correct
black-height; every path *through* `x` is short by exactly one black node. `w = x->parent's
other child` is never `t->nil`, since black-height parity forces `w`'s subtree to have height
≥1 whenever `x` is doubly-black.

- **Case 1 — `w` is red.** Recolor `w` black, `x->parent` red, left-rotate at `x->parent`.
  *Invariant restored:* none of the deficiency is fixed yet — this is a pure setup step that
  makes `w` black, satisfying cases 2–4's precondition. Black-height is preserved because the
  rotation and the `w`/parent color swap exactly cancel: every path's black-count through this
  local subtree is unchanged, only relabeled.
- **Case 2 — `w` black, both of `w`'s children black.** Recolor `w` red (no rotation).
  *Invariant restored:* the deficiency moves from `x` up to `x->parent` — `w`'s subtree now has
  one less black on every path, matching `x`'s existing shortfall, so `x->parent`'s two subtrees
  agree again, with the shortfall now sitting at `x->parent`. Loop continues with `x =
  x->parent` (or exits immediately/absorbs-for-free if the new `x` is red).
- **Case 3 — `w` black, `w->left` red, `w->right` black.** Recolor `w->left` black, `w` red,
  right-rotate at `w`. *Invariant restored:* purely local to `w`'s subtree — `x`'s deficiency is
  untouched, but `x`'s sibling is now the old `w->left`, whose *far* child (the old `w`, now red)
  is red — the precondition for case 4. Black-height preserved by the same rotation+color-swap
  cancellation as case 1.
- **Case 4 — `w` black, `w->right` red (terminating case).** `w` takes `x->parent`'s color,
  `x->parent` becomes black, `w->right` becomes black, left-rotate at `x->parent`. Set `x =
  t->root` to end the loop. *Invariant restored:* fully eliminates the deficiency — `x->parent`
  becoming black supplies the exact black `x`'s path was missing, while `w` inheriting
  `x->parent`'s old color and `w->right` turning black exactly offset the structural shift from
  the rotation on every other path.

Mirror cases (x is `parent`'s **right** child): swap `left`/`right` and `w = x->parent->left`
throughout. This is the single highest-risk place to introduce a copy-paste bug (see Risks).

# 4. Where the key copy and value are freed — every path

| Path | Key freed | Value freed | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Key not found | never | never | Return -1 immediately after the search walk; no mutation. |
| `z` has 0 or 1 child (`y == z`) | `free(z->key)` in step 6 | `t->value_free(z->value)` (if non-NULL) in step 6 | Exactly once each, right before freeing the `z` struct. |
| `z` has 2 children (`y != z`, "overwrite" path) | `free(z->key)` **in step 2**, immediately before `z->key = y->key` | `t->value_free(z->value)` **in step 2**, immediately before `z->value = y->value` | `z`'s *original* key/value are what the caller asked to delete — must be freed before being overwritten by the successor's, or they leak. `y->key`/`y->value` are transferred (pointer move), never duplicated and never freed directly — set `y->key = y->value = NULL` right after the transfer as a defensive guard. |

Ordering is the highest-risk detail in the whole function: free-before-overwrite in step 2, and
never call `value_free` on `y`'s value in the 2-child path (it now belongs to `z`). Since
`rb_delete` performs zero allocations, CLAUDE.md's goto-cleanup pattern (for multi-allocation
functions) doesn't apply here — the only early-exit is the "not found" `-1` return before any
mutation happens.

# 5. Table-driven tests (priority order)

Requires a new test-only header, **`src/rbtree_internal.h`** (not part of the graded
`include/rbtree.h` contract — CLAUDE.md only forbids modifying that file), exposing `rb_node_t`
/ `struct rbtree` so `tests/test_rbtree.c` can build exact tree shapes directly and call
`rb_delete` + `rb_validate` on them, rather than depending on `rb_insert`'s fixup behavior to
indirectly produce each shape.

Write in this order:
1. Delete from empty tree → -1, tree unchanged.
2. Delete non-existent key from non-empty tree → -1, size unchanged, `rb_validate() == 0`.
3. Delete the only node (root) → tree empty, `root == nil`, `size == 0`.
4. Value-ownership spy test: a `value_free` that records call count + freed pointers; assert
   it's called exactly once per deleted key, never for surviving keys, never twice on one
   pointer. This is the direct regression test for section 4's free-before-overwrite ordering.
5. Delete a red leaf (no fixup entered).
6. Delete a black leaf, sibling red → Case 1 → chains into 2/3/4 (white-box constructed).
7. Delete a black node, sibling black + both sibling's children black, in a tree ≥3 levels
   tall → Case 2, verify the deficiency actually propagates upward across levels (not just
   terminates after one step).
8. Delete a black node, sibling black, near-red/far-black child → Case 3 → 4 transition.
9. Delete a black node, sibling black, far-red child directly → Case 4 immediately.
10. Mirror versions of 6–9 with `x` as a **right** child — catches left/right copy-paste bugs.
11. Two-children delete where successor is `z->right` directly (`y->parent == z` shortcut path).
12. Two-children delete where successor is deeper (`transplant(y, y->right)` general path).
13. Delete the root when it has two children — confirms `t->root` reassignment and final
    "root must be black" recoloring.
14. Repeated deletes down to empty, calling `rb_validate()` + checking `rb_size()` after
    *every single* delete — catches bugs that only manifest operations later.
15. `make asan` / `make memcheck` pass over a insert-N/delete-in-random-order run — leak/UB
    backstop across all of 1–14 combined.

# Risks

- **Depends on `rb_insert` / `rb_create` / `rb_validate` / the internal struct existing and
  matching this design.** None of them exist yet. White-box tests (via
  `src/rbtree_internal.h`) can validate delete's structural correctness in isolation, but true
  end-to-end coverage (insert-then-delete via the public API only) needs `rb_insert` implemented
  with this same sentinel-nil representation.
- **`tests/fuzz.c`** is referenced by the Makefile (`make test` builds `$(FUZZBIN)` from it) but
  doesn't exist yet — unrelated to this plan's scope, but `make test` will fail to build until
  it's created by whoever implements it.
- **Left/right mirror duplication** in the fixup cases is the single most likely place to
  introduce a subtle bug (copy-paste with an unswapped `left`/`right`) — test #10 exists
  specifically to catch this and should not be skipped or treated as redundant with #6–9.
- **Copy-into-z strategy** is a deliberate deviation from literal CLRS pseudocode (which
  relinks the successor node itself rather than copying key/value). Flagging in case the
  assignment's rubric expects the textbook structural version specifically.
- **`rb_validate`'s exact invariant checks aren't implemented yet either** — this plan assumes
  it checks: root is black, no red node has a red child, equal black-height on every root-to-nil
  path, and valid BST key ordering. If that's not what gets built, tests 6–14 (which lean on it
  as the oracle) need re-checking against whatever it actually verifies.

# Context

`rb_delete` needs to be designed before it's implemented, per CLAUDE.md's workflow rule
("For any multi-file or algorithmic change: propose a plan and wait for approval before
editing"). `src/rbtree.c` is currently empty (only a placeholder comment) and
`tests/test_rbtree.c` is empty. `include/rbtree.h` (off-limits, graded contract) documents
`rb_delete` as: "Removes key; frees the key copy and the value. Returns 0, or -1 if absent."

This plan assumes `rb_create`/`rb_insert`/`rb_validate` and the internal node representation
will exist by the time `rb_delete` is implemented (built separately, not in this plan) — the
internal design proposed here (sentinel-nil, node fields) must be the same one `rb_insert`
uses, since both share it.

# 1. Internal representation (shared prerequisite, not exposed via rbtree.h)

```c
typedef enum { RB_RED, RB_BLACK } rb_color_t;

typedef struct rb_node {
    char *key;
    void *value;
    rb_color_t color;
    struct rb_node *parent, *left, *right;
} rb_node_t;

struct rbtree {
    rb_node_t *root;
    rb_node_t *nil;          /* sentinel: always black, parent/left/right unused */
    rb_value_free_fn value_free;
    size_t size;
};
```

Sentinel `nil` (CLRS-style) means every "child" pointer is always a valid node whose `->color`
is readable — avoids scattering NULL-guards through the fixup logic. `t->nil->color` must stay
`RB_BLACK` for the tree's lifetime.

# 2. Transplant + successor strategy

`rb_transplant(t, u, v)`: standard — replaces the subtree rooted at `u` with the subtree rooted
at `v` by rewiring `u->parent`'s child pointer to `v` and setting `v->parent = u->parent` (`v`
may be `t->nil`).

`rb_delete(t, key)`:
1. Find `z` via the same search walk `rb_find` uses. If not found, return -1 (no mutation, no
   frees — delete never allocates, so there is no "leave tree unchanged on OOM" concern here at
   all, only "leave tree unchanged when key is absent").
2. Determine the node to physically unlink, `y`:
   - If `z` has ≤1 child: `y = z`.
   - If `z` has 2 children: `y = tree_minimum(z->right)` (in-order successor). **Free `z`'s
     original key/value now** (this is the moment the caller's requested key is actually
     removed), then transfer (not duplicate) `y->key`/`y->value` into `z->key`/`z->value`. `y`
     is now unlinked as a structural shell — its key/value fields are set to NULL immediately
     after the transfer so a future refactor can't double-free them.
3. `x` = `y`'s only child (`y` has ≤1 child by construction — either it's `z` with ≤1 child, or
   it's a successor, which never has a left child). `y_original_color = y->color`.
4. `rb_transplant(t, y, x)` — **one unconditional call, no `y->parent == z` special case.**
   This is a deliberate difference from literal CLRS: in the textbook relink strategy, `y`
   physically moves into `z`'s position, so when `y == z->right` a naive transplant would try to
   set `y->right = z->right` — but `z->right` *is* `y`, creating a self-loop, hence CLRS's
   explicit `if (y->parent == z) x->parent = y;` carve-out. Under copy-into-z, `z` never moves —
   `y` is only ever discarded after its key/value are stripped out in step 2 — so `transplant(y,
   x)` alone is correct in both cases:
   - `y == z->right` directly: `transplant` sees `y == y->parent->right`, sets `z->right = x`
     and `x->parent = z`; `z->left` is untouched. `x`'s sibling (for the fixup loop) is
     correctly `z->left`.
   - `y` is deeper down `z->right`'s left-spine (`y->parent != z`): `transplant` sets
     `y->parent->left = x` and `x->parent = y->parent`; `z->right`/`z->left` are both untouched.
   Either way, `x->parent` ends up correct so `rb_delete_fixup` can find `w` from the right spot.
5. If `z != y`: `y` inherits `z`'s structural role — set `y->left = z->left`, `y->right =
   z->right`, `y->color = z->color`, fix both children's `->parent`, and fix `z`'s old parent's
   child pointer to point at `y` (or update `t->root` if `z` was root). *(Only needed if using
   relink; skipped entirely under the copy-into-z strategy below since `z` never moves.)*
6. If `z == y` (0/1-child case): free `z->key`, call `t->value_free(z->value)` if
   `value_free != NULL`, then free the `z` node struct itself.
   If `z != y` (2-child case): `z`'s key/value were already freed and overwritten in step 2;
   free `y`'s now-empty node struct only (no key/value to free — already transferred/NULLed).
7. If `y_original_color == RB_BLACK`: `rb_delete_fixup(t, x)`.
8. `t->size--`; return 0.

**Chosen strategy (per your answer): copy-into-z.** `z` never moves — its key/value fields get
overwritten with the successor's, and the *successor node* (which structurally has ≤1 child) is
the one spliced out via `rb_transplant`. This keeps all pointer surgery confined to the
single-child-unlink case (step 4/5 collapses to just the transplant, no step-5 relink needed) and
avoids the classic "z->key lives in freed memory" bug from the textbook relink version. Since
`rb_node_t` never escapes the opaque public API, no caller can hold a stale pointer to the old
`z` identity, so this deviation from literal CLRS pseudocode is safe.

# 3. Deletion-fixup cases (x is `parent`'s **left** child; mirror for right — see risk below)

Loop invariant on entry to each iteration: `x` is "doubly-black" (or singly-red, which the loop
condition `x != root && x->color == BLACK` catches and just exits, then `x->color = RB_BLACK`
after the loop absorbs it for free) — every root-to-leaf path *not* through `x` has correct
black-height; every path *through* `x` is short by exactly one black node. `w = x->parent's
other child` is never `t->nil`, since black-height parity forces `w`'s subtree to have height
≥1 whenever `x` is doubly-black.

- **Case 1 — `w` is red.** Recolor `w` black, `x->parent` red, left-rotate at `x->parent`.
  *Invariant restored:* none of the deficiency is fixed yet — this is a pure setup step that
  makes `w` black, satisfying cases 2–4's precondition. Black-height is preserved because the
  rotation and the `w`/parent color swap exactly cancel: every path's black-count through this
  local subtree is unchanged, only relabeled.
- **Case 2 — `w` black, both of `w`'s children black.** Recolor `w` red (no rotation).
  *Invariant restored:* the deficiency moves from `x` up to `x->parent` — `w`'s subtree now has
  one less black on every path, matching `x`'s existing shortfall, so `x->parent`'s two subtrees
  agree again, with the shortfall now sitting at `x->parent`. Loop continues with `x =
  x->parent` (or exits immediately/absorbs-for-free if the new `x` is red).
- **Case 3 — `w` black, `w->left` red, `w->right` black.** Recolor `w->left` black, `w` red,
  right-rotate at `w`. *Invariant restored:* purely local to `w`'s subtree — `x`'s deficiency is
  untouched, but `x`'s sibling is now the old `w->left`, whose *far* child (the old `w`, now red)
  is red — the precondition for case 4. Black-height preserved by the same rotation+color-swap
  cancellation as case 1.
- **Case 4 — `w` black, `w->right` red (terminating case).** `w` takes `x->parent`'s color,
  `x->parent` becomes black, `w->right` becomes black, left-rotate at `x->parent`. Set `x =
  t->root` to end the loop. *Invariant restored:* fully eliminates the deficiency — `x->parent`
  becoming black supplies the exact black `x`'s path was missing, while `w` inheriting
  `x->parent`'s old color and `w->right` turning black exactly offset the structural shift from
  the rotation on every other path.

Mirror cases (x is `parent`'s **right** child): swap `left`/`right` and `w = x->parent->left`
throughout. This is the single highest-risk place to introduce a copy-paste bug (see Risks).

# 4. Where the key copy and value are freed — every path

| Path | Key freed | Value freed | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Key not found | never | never | Return -1 immediately after the search walk; no mutation. |
| `z` has 0 or 1 child (`y == z`) | `free(z->key)` in step 6 | `t->value_free(z->value)` (if non-NULL) in step 6 | Exactly once each, right before freeing the `z` struct. |
| `z` has 2 children (`y != z`, "overwrite" path) | `free(z->key)` **in step 2**, immediately before `z->key = y->key` | `t->value_free(z->value)` **in step 2**, immediately before `z->value = y->value` | `z`'s *original* key/value are what the caller asked to delete — must be freed before being overwritten by the successor's, or they leak. `y->key`/`y->value` are transferred (pointer move), never duplicated and never freed directly — set `y->key = y->value = NULL` right after the transfer as a defensive guard. |

Ordering is the highest-risk detail in the whole function: free-before-overwrite in step 2, and
never call `value_free` on `y`'s value in the 2-child path (it now belongs to `z`). Since
`rb_delete` performs zero allocations, CLAUDE.md's goto-cleanup pattern (for multi-allocation
functions) doesn't apply here — the only early-exit is the "not found" `-1` return before any
mutation happens.

# 5. Table-driven tests (priority order)

Requires a new test-only header, **`src/rbtree_internal.h`** (not part of the graded
`include/rbtree.h` contract — CLAUDE.md only forbids modifying that file), exposing `rb_node_t`
/ `struct rbtree` so `tests/test_rbtree.c` can build exact tree shapes directly and call
`rb_delete` + `rb_validate` on them, rather than depending on `rb_insert`'s fixup behavior to
indirectly produce each shape.

Write in this order:
1. Delete from empty tree → -1, tree unchanged.
2. Delete non-existent key from non-empty tree → -1, size unchanged, `rb_validate() == 0`.
3. Delete the only node (root) → tree empty, `root == nil`, `size == 0`.
4. Value-ownership spy test: a `value_free` that records call count + freed pointers; assert
   it's called exactly once per deleted key, never for surviving keys, never twice on one
   pointer. This is the direct regression test for section 4's free-before-overwrite ordering.
5. Delete a red leaf (no fixup entered).
6. Delete a black leaf, sibling red → Case 1 → chains into 2/3/4 (white-box constructed).
7. Delete a black node, sibling black + both sibling's children black, in a tree ≥3 levels

   terminates after one step).
8. Delete a black node, sibling black, near-red/far-black child → Case 3 → 4 transition.
9. Delete a black node, sibling black, far-red child directly → Case 4 immediately.
10. Mirror versions of 6–9 with `x` as a **right** child — catches left/right copy-paste bugs.
11. Two-children delete where successor is `z->right` directly (`y->parent == z` shortcut path).
12. Two-children delete where successor is deeper (`transplant(y, y->right)` general path).
13. Delete the root when it has two children — confirms `t->root` reassignment and final

  `src/rbtree_internal.h`) can validate delete's structural correctness in isolation, but true

The balancing phase can't leak, by construction — here's why, and I'll make it explicit in the plan.

**`rb_delete_fixup` (and the `rotate_left`/`rotate_right` helpers it calls) never call `malloc` or `free`.** The entire balancing phase is pointer reassignment and color flips among nodes already live in the tree — recoloring `w`, rotating at `x->parent` or `w`, moving `x` up. There is nothing for it to leak, because it never takes ownership of anything new or releases anything.

The only place `rb_delete` frees memory is step 6 (freeing `z`'s or `y`'s key/value/struct), and that happens **before** step 7 calls the fixup — critically, on a node that step 4's `transplant` has already fully unlinked from the tree. So by the time fixup runs:
- `x` and everything reachable from it (`x->parent`, `w`, etc.) are live nodes still in the tree — never the just-freed one.
- The freed pointer (`y`, or `z` in the 0/1-child case) isn't reachable from anywhere fixup walks, so there's no use-after-free risk either, not just no leak.

The one thing to guard explicitly: **`t->nil` must never be freed** by delete or fixup — it's allocated once in `rb_create` and freed once in `rb_destroy`. Fixup does write to `t->nil->parent` as scratch space (via `transplant` when `x == t->nil`, so the loop can walk up from the right place) — that's expected and fine, but `t->nil->color` must never be changed, and nothing should ever call `free(t->nil)` or `free(x)` where `x` could alias the sentinel.

Verification backstop: this is exactly what `make asan` and `make memcheck` (already in the Makefile) are for — ASAN catches use-after-free immediately, valgrind's `--leak-check=full` catches any leaked byte. Test #15 (insert-N/delete-random-order under both) is the dedicated regression net for this; I'd also add a lightweight debug-only assertion after every `rb_delete` call in the white-box tests that `t->nil->color == RB_BLACK` and `t->nil->left == t->nil->right == t->nil`, since a fixup bug that accidentally treats the sentinel as a normal mutable node would corrupt it silently and only manifest as a weird failure much later.

`rb_delete` as: "Removes key; frees the key copy and the value. Returns 0, or -1 if absent."

This plan assumes `rb_create`/`rb_insert`/`rb_validate` and the internal node representation
will exist by the time `rb_delete` is implemented (built separately, not in this plan) — the
internal design proposed here (sentinel-nil, node fields) must be the same one `rb_insert`
uses, since both share it.

# 1. Internal representation (shared prerequisite, not exposed via rbtree.h)

```c
typedef enum { RB_RED, RB_BLACK } rb_color_t;

typedef struct rb_node {
    char *key;
    void *value;
    rb_color_t color;
    struct rb_node *parent, *left, *right;
} rb_node_t;

struct rbtree {
    rb_node_t *root;
    rb_node_t *nil;          /* sentinel: always black, parent/left/right unused */
    rb_value_free_fn value_free;
    size_t size;
};
```

Sentinel `nil` (CLRS-style) means every "child" pointer is always a valid node whose `->color`
is readable — avoids scattering NULL-guards through the fixup logic. `t->nil->color` must stay
`RB_BLACK` for the tree's lifetime.

# 2. Transplant + successor strategy

`rb_transplant(t, u, v)`: standard — replaces the subtree rooted at `u` with the subtree rooted
at `v` by rewiring `u->parent`'s child pointer to `v` and setting `v->parent = u->parent` (`v`
may be `t->nil`).

`rb_delete(t, key)`:
1. Find `z` via the same search walk `rb_find` uses. If not found, return -1 (no mutation, no
   frees — delete never allocates, so there is no "leave tree unchanged on OOM" concern here at
   all, only "leave tree unchanged when key is absent").
2. Determine the node to physically unlink, `y`:
   - If `z` has ≤1 child: `y = z`.
   - If `z` has 2 children: `y = tree_minimum(z->right)` (in-order successor). **Free `z`'s
     original key/value now** (this is the moment the caller's requested key is actually
     removed), then transfer (not duplicate) `y->key`/`y->value` into `z->key`/`z->value`. `y`
     is now unlinked as a structural shell — its key/value fields are set to NULL immediately
     after the transfer so a future refactor can't double-free them.
3. `x` = `y`'s only child (`y` has ≤1 child by construction — either it's `z` with ≤1 child, or
   it's a successor, which never has a left child). `y_original_color = y->color`.
4. `rb_transplant(t, y, x)` — **one unconditional call, no `y->parent == z` special case.**
   This is a deliberate difference from literal CLRS: in the textbook relink strategy, `y`
   physically moves into `z`'s position, so when `y == z->right` a naive transplant would try to
   set `y->right = z->right` — but `z->right` *is* `y`, creating a self-loop, hence CLRS's
   explicit `if (y->parent == z) x->parent = y;` carve-out. Under copy-into-z, `z` never moves —
   `y` is only ever discarded after its key/value are stripped out in step 2 — so `transplant(y,
   x)` alone is correct in both cases:

     and `x->parent = z`; `z->left` is untouched. `x`'s sibling (for the fixup loop) is
     correctly `z->left`.

editing"). `src/rbtree.c` is currently empty (only a placeholder comment) and
`tests/test_rbtree.c` is empty. `include/rbtree.h` (off-limits, graded contract) documents
`rb_delete` as: "Removes key; frees the key copy and the value. Returns 0, or -1 if absent."

This plan assumes `rb_create`/`rb_insert`/`rb_validate` and the internal node representation
will exist by the time `rb_delete` is implemented (built separately, not in this plan) — the
internal design proposed here (sentinel-nil, node fields) must be the same one `rb_insert`
uses, since both share it.

# 1. Internal representation (shared prerequisite, not exposed via rbtree.h)

```c
typedef enum { RB_RED, RB_BLACK } rb_color_t;

typedef struct rb_node {
    char *key;
    void *value;
    rb_color_t color;
    struct rb_node *parent, *left, *right;
} rb_node_t;

struct rbtree {
    rb_node_t *root;
    rb_node_t *nil;          /* sentinel: always black, parent/left/right unused */
    rb_value_free_fn value_free;
    size_t size;
};
```

Sentinel `nil` (CLRS-style) means every "child" pointer is always a valid node whose `->color`
is readable — avoids scattering NULL-guards through the fixup logic. `t->nil->color` must stay
`RB_BLACK` for the tree's lifetime.

# 2. Transplant + successor strategy

`rb_transplant(t, u, v)`: standard — replaces the subtree rooted at `u` with the subtree rooted
at `v` by rewiring `u->parent`'s child pointer to `v` and setting `v->parent = u->parent` (`v`
may be `t->nil`).

`rb_delete(t, key)`:
1. Find `z` via the same search walk `rb_find` uses. If not found, return -1 (no mutation, no
   frees — delete never allocates, so there is no "leave tree unchanged on OOM" concern here at
   all, only "leave tree unchanged when key is absent").
2. Determine the node to physically unlink, `y`:
   - If `z` has ≤1 child: `y = z`.
   - If `z` has 2 children: `y = tree_minimum(z->right)` (in-order successor). **Free `z`'s
     original key/value now** (this is the moment the caller's requested key is actually
     removed), then transfer (not duplicate) `y->key`/`y->value` into `z->key`/`z->value`. `y`
     is now unlinked as a structural shell — its key/value fields are set to NULL immediately
     after the transfer so a future refactor can't double-free them.
3. `x` = `y`'s only child (`y` has ≤1 child by construction — either it's `z` with ≤1 child, or
   it's a successor, which never has a left child). `y_original_color = y->color`.
4. `rb_transplant(t, y, x)` — **one unconditional call, no `y->parent == z` special case.**
   This is a deliberate difference from literal CLRS: in the textbook relink strategy, `y`
   physically moves into `z`'s position, so when `y == z->right` a naive transplant would try to
   set `y->right = z->right` — but `z->right` *is* `y`, creating a self-loop, hence CLRS's
   explicit `if (y->parent == z) x->parent = y;` carve-out. Under copy-into-z, `z` never moves —
   `y` is only ever discarded after its key/value are stripped out in step 2 — so `transplant(y,
   x)` alone is correct in both cases:
   - `y == z->right` directly: `transplant` sees `y == y->parent->right`, sets `z->right = x`
     and `x->parent = z`; `z->left` is untouched. `x`'s sibling (for the fixup loop) is
     correctly `z->left`.
   - `y` is deeper down `z->right`'s left-spine (`y->parent != z`): `transplant` sets
     `y->parent->left = x` and `x->parent = y->parent`; `z->right`/`z->left` are both untouched.
   Either way, `x->parent` ends up correct so `rb_delete_fixup` can find `w` from the right spot.
5. If `z != y`: `y` inherits `z`'s structural role — set `y->left = z->left`, `y->right =
   z->right`, `y->color = z->color`, fix both children's `->parent`, and fix `z`'s old parent's
   child pointer to point at `y` (or update `t->root` if `z` was root). *(Only needed if using
   relink; skipped entirely under the copy-into-z strategy below since `z` never moves.)*
6. If `z == y` (0/1-child case): free `z->key`, call `t->value_free(z->value)` if
   `value_free != NULL`, then free the `z` node struct itself.
   If `z != y` (2-child case): `z`'s key/value were already freed and overwritten in step 2;
   free `y`'s now-empty node struct only (no key/value to free — already transferred/NULLed).
7. If `y_original_color == RB_BLACK`: `rb_delete_fixup(t, x)`.
8. `t->size--`; return 0.

**Chosen strategy (per your answer): copy-into-z.** `z` never moves — its key/value fields get
overwritten with the successor's, and the *successor node* (which structurally has ≤1 child) is
the one spliced out via `rb_transplant`. This keeps all pointer surgery confined to the
single-child-unlink case (step 4/5 collapses to just the transplant, no step-5 relink needed) and

content.text:
# Fewer Permission Prompts

Look through my transcripts' MCP and bash tool calls, and based on those, make a prioritized list of patterns that I should add to my permission allowlist to reduce permission prompts. Focus on read-only commands.

The format for permissions is: `Bash(foo*)`, `Bash(foo)`, `Bash(foo bar *)`, `mcp__slack__slack_read_thread`, etc.

Then, add these to the project `.claude/settings.json` under `permissions.allow`.

## Steps

1. **Locate transcripts.** Session transcripts live at `~/.claude/projects/<sanitized-cwd>/*.jsonl`. Each line is a JSON object. Tool calls appear as `assistant` messages with `message.content[]` entries of `type: "tool_use"`. The `name` field identifies the tool (e.g. `"Bash"`, `"mcp__slack__slack_read_thread"`); for Bash, `input.command` is the shell string.

   Scan the recent transcripts across the user's projects dir — not just the current project — so the allowlist reflects their actual usage. Cap the scan at a reasonable number of recent sessions (e.g. 50 most-recently-modified JSONL files) so this stays fast.

2. **Extract tool-call frequencies.**
   - For `Bash` calls: parse `input.command`, take the leading command token (handling `sudo`, `timeout`, pipes, `&&`, env-var prefixes). Record the command + first subcommand pair (e.g. `git status`, `gh pr view`, `ls`, `cat`).
   - For MCP calls: record the full tool name (e.g. `mcp__slack__slack_read_thread`).
   - Count occurrences across the scanned transcripts.

3. **Filter to read-only.** Keep only commands that don't mutate state. Examples of read-only: `ls`, `cat`, `pwd`, `git status`, `git log`, `git diff`, `git show`, `git branch`, `rg`, `grep`, `find`, `head`, `tail`, `wc`, `file`, `which`, `echo`, `date`, `gh pr view`, `gh pr list`, `gh pr diff`, `gh issue view`, `gh issue list`, `gh run list`, `gh run view`, `gh api` (GET), `bun run typecheck`, `bun run lint`, `bun run test` (for tests that don't mutate), `docker ps`, `docker logs`, `kubectl get`, `kubectl describe`, `ps`, `top`, `df`, `du`, `env`, `printenv`, any MCP tool with `read`/`get`/`list`/`search`/`view` in its name.

   Drop anything that writes, deletes, renames, pushes, merges, installs, or runs a build/test that has side effects. When in doubt, leave it out.

   **Never allowlist a pattern that grants arbitrary code execution.** A wildcard rule for any of these (e.g. `Bash(python3:*)`) is equivalent to allowing arbitrary code execution. This list is not exhaustive — apply the same rule to anything in the same category:
   - Interpreters: `python`/`python3`, `node`, `bun`, `deno`, `ruby`, `perl`, `php`, `lua`, etc.
   - Shells: `bash`, `sh`, `zsh`, `fish`, `eval`, `exec`, `ssh`, etc.
   - Package runners: `npx`, `bunx`, `uvx`, `uv run`, etc.
   - Task-runner wildcards: `npm run *`, `yarn run *`, `pnpm run *`, `bun run *`, `make *`, `just *`, `cargo run *`, `go run *`, etc. — an exact `Bash(bun run typecheck)` is fine, `Bash(bun run *)` is not
   - `gh api *`, `docker run`/`exec`, `kubectl exec`, `sudo`, and similar

4. **Drop commands Claude Code already auto-allows.** These don't need an allowlist entry — they never prompt. If you see any of these in the transcripts, skip them; don't suggest them to the user.

   - **Always auto-allowed (any args):** `cal`, `uptime`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `wc`, `stat`, `strings`, `hexdump`, `od`, `nl`, `id`, `uname`, `free`, `df`, `du`, `locale`, `groups`, `nproc`, `basename`, `dirname`, `realpath`, `cut`, `paste`, `tr`, `column`, `tac`, `rev`, `fold`, `expand`, `unexpand`, `fmt`, `comm`, `cmp`, `numfmt`, `readlink`, `diff`, `true`, `false`, `sleep`, `which`, `type`, `expr`, `seq`, `tsort`, `pr`, `echo`, `ls`, `cd`.
   - **Auto-allowed with zero args only:** `pwd`, `whoami`, `alias`.
   - **Auto-allowed exact forms:** `claude -h`, `claude --help`, `node -v`, `node --version`, `python --version`, `python3 --version`, `ip addr`.
   - **Auto-allowed with safe flags only (validated):** `xargs`, `file`, `sed` (read-only expressions), `sort`, `man`, `help`, `netstat`, `ps`, `base64`, `grep`, `egrep`, `fgrep`, `sha256sum`, `sha1sum`, `md5sum`, `tree`, `date`, `hostname`, `lsof`, `pgrep`, `tput`, `ss`, `fd`, `fdfind`, `aki`, `rg`, `jq`, `uniq`, `history`, `arch`, `ifconfig`, `pyright`, `find` (blocks `-delete`/`-exec`/`-execdir`/`-ok`/`-okdir`/`-fprint*`/`-fls`/`-files0-from`), `printf` (blocks any `-flag`), `test` (blocks `-v`/`-R`/`-a`/`-o`).
   - **All git read-only subcommands:** `git status`, `git log`, `git diff`, `git show`, `git blame`, `git branch`, `git tag`, `git remote`, `git ls-files`, `git ls-remote`, `git config --get`, `git rev-parse`, `git describe`, `git stash list`, `git reflog`, `git shortlog`, `git cat-file`, `git for-each-ref`, `git worktree list`, etc.
   - **All gh read-only subcommands:** `gh pr view`, `gh pr list`, `gh pr diff`, `gh pr checks`, `gh pr status`, `gh issue view`, `gh issue list`, `gh issue status`, `gh run view`, `gh run list`, `gh workflow list`, `gh workflow view`, `gh repo view`, `gh release view`, `gh release list`, `gh api` (GET), `gh auth status`, etc.
   - **Docker read-only subcommands:** `docker ps`, `docker images`, `docker logs`, `docker inspect`.

   Source of truth: `src/tools/BashTool/readOnlyValidation.ts` (`READONLY_COMMANDS`, `READONLY_NOARGS`, `READONLY_EXACT`, `COMMAND_ALLOWLIST`) and `src/utils/shell/readOnlyCommandValidation.ts` (`GIT_READ_ONLY_COMMANDS`, `GH_READ_ONLY_COMMANDS`, `DOCKER_READ_ONLY_COMMANDS`, `RIPGREP_READ_ONLY_COMMANDS`, `PYRIGHT_READ_ONLY_COMMANDS`). If the user is in this repo and you're unsure whether a command is covered, grep these files rather than guessing.

5. **Pick the pattern form.** Use the narrowest pattern that still covers the observed usage:
   - If the user runs many variants (`git log`, `git log --oneline`, `git log main..HEAD`): use `Bash(git log *)` — note the space before `*`, which is required for prefix matching to work correctly.
   - If a single exact invocation is common: use `Bash(foo)` with no wildcard.
   - For MCP: use the full tool name verbatim (no wildcard needed; they're already specific).
   - Never widen a pattern to the point that it conflicts with the rules above (no arbitrary code execution, no mutation/side effects).

6. **Prioritize.** Rank by count descending. Drop anything that appeared fewer than ~3 times — not worth the allowlist entry. Cap the list at the top ~20 so the user can skim it.

7. **Present the prioritized list to the user** as a markdown table with columns: rank, pattern, count, one-line description. Example:

   | # | Pattern | Count | Notes |
   |---|---------|-------|-------|
   | 1 | `Bash(git status *)` | 142 | repo status checks |
   | 2 | `Bash(gh pr view *)` | 87 | PR inspection |
   | 3 | `mcp__slack__slack_read_thread` | 54 | Slack thread reads |

8. **Merge into `.claude/settings.json`** in the current project (not `~/.claude/settings.json`, not `.claude/settings.local.json`). Create the file if it doesn't exist. Preserve existing keys and existing entries in `permissions.allow`; de-duplicate against what's already there; don't remove anything; don't reorder unrelated fields.

9. **Report back.** Tell the user what you added (count + a few examples), what was already in the allowlist, and what you skipped and why (e.g. "dropped `rm` and `git push` — not read-only; dropped `cat`/`ls`/`git status` — already auto-allowed, no rule needed").

Do not add anything to `permissions.deny` or `permissions.ask`. Do not touch any other settings field.

**`rb_transplant`** — this is the splice-out mechanic the two-children case actually needs. After I copy the successor `y`'s key/value into `z` (per the copy-into-z strategy from the plan we agreed on), `y` itself — a node with at most one child, `x = y->right` — has to be physically removed from the tree structure. `rb_transplant(t, y, x)` does exactly that: it finds whichever pointer currently points at `y` (either `t->root` if `y` were root, or `y->parent->left`/`y->parent->right`) and redirects it to `x`, then sets `x->parent` correctly — including the case where `x` is the `nil` sentinel. This is the exact helper named in section 2 of the plan you approved ("`rb_transplant(t, u, v)`: standard — replaces the subtree rooted at `u`..."). Here's the full breakdown of what I proposed, piece by piece:

**`rotate_left` / `rotate_right`** — the two rebalancing primitives every fixup case depends on. A rotation locally restructures three pointers (a node, its child, and that child's inner grandchild) while preserving BST ordering. I need both directions because fixup cases 1 and 3 rotate at different points depending on which side the deficient node is on. I wrote them as the standard CLRS pointer-surgery: pull up the child (`y = x->right` for left-rotate), hand its inner subtree back to `x`, then swap parent links — including the `x->parent == t->nil` check so it correctly updates `t->root` when rotating at the root. These are pure pointer/color operations, no allocation, matching the "fixup never allocates" memory-safety argument from the plan we agreed on earlier.

**`rb_delete_fixup`** — implements the four cases (and their left/right mirrors) from that same plan. I chose the `while (x != t->root && x->color == RB_BLACK)` loop structure directly from the design because it encodes the termination conditions concisely: the loop naturally exits when `x` reaches the root (deficiency absorbed at the top) or when `x` picks up red along the way (Case 2's "parent was red" sub-case falls out for free — no separate branch needed, it's just the loop condition failing on the next check). Inside, each `if`/`else` pair mirrors the case exactly as documented: Case 1 (red sibling → recolor+rotate to expose a black sibling), Case 2 (both nephews black → recolor sibling red, push `x` up), Case 3 (near nephew red → recolor+rotate to set up Case 4), Case 4 (far nephew red → recolor+rotate, terminate by setting `x = t->root`). I didn't factor out a shared helper for the left/right mirrors — CLRS-style duplication here is the standard tradeoff (a generic version needs function pointers or extra indirection for `left`/`right` field access, which reads worse for something this short); the mirror-bug risk this creates was already flagged in the plan's Risks section, which is exactly why the test table has a dedicated mirror case.

**`rb_delete` restructuring** — I split the single `if (has 0/1 children)` early-return into the two real branches CLRS distinguishes (`z->left == t->nil` vs `z->right == t->nil`), because they need different transplants (`rb_transplant(t, z, z->right)` vs `rb_transplant(t, z, z->left)`) and, unlike the two-children case, `z` itself is the node that gets unlinked and freed here — there's no successor to copy from. I kept the existing two-children branch's copy-into-z logic completely unchanged (same free-before-overwrite ordering as before), just moved it into the `else` arm. The new unifying piece is `y_original_color`: CLRS's insight is that only the *physically removed* node's original color matters for deciding whether fixup runs — in the 0/1-child branch that's `z` itself, in the two-children branch it's the successor `y` — so I capture it once (`y = z` initially, reassigned only in the two-children branch) and check it once at the end (`if (y_original_color == RB_BLACK) rb_delete_fixup(t, x)`), rather than duplicating that check three times.
